title: Why Liechtenstein Is Tiny but Secretly Rich
hook: One of the richest countries on Earth has no army, no airport, and a prince who bought it without ever setting foot in it.
era: Holy Roman Empire, Alpine Europe, about 1700
thumbnail_picture: Huge close view on the right of a small Alpine castle on a steep green hill above a valley, glowing in golden light, with a stack of gold coins in the foreground; a wide-eyed European nobleman in a powdered wig and velvet coat, early 1700s, stares at it in astonishment. Left third is empty sky.

scenes.narration: One of the richest countries on Earth has no army, no airport, and was bought by a prince who never visited.
scenes.caption: LIECHTENSTEIN
scenes.picture: Wide sunny view of a tiny Alpine country: a hilltop castle above a small town in a green valley, snowy mountains behind, clear blue sky

scenes.narration: So how does a speck in the Alps, with about forty thousand people, end up this rich?
scenes.caption: 40,000 PEOPLE
scenes.picture: A tiny green valley squeezed between two huge snowy mountain walls, seen from high above, a thin river running through it

scenes.narration: The answer starts with a prince, a shopping spree, and one very badly wanted seat at a table.
scenes.caption: THE SHOPPING SPREE
scenes.picture: A wealthy European prince in a powdered wig and red velvet coat smiles slyly, holding a heavy purse of coins, grand palace hall behind him

scenes.narration: But first, the size. You could drive the whole country, end to end, in about half an hour.
scenes.caption: 25 KM LONG
scenes.picture: A small car driving along a straight valley road, a river on one side and steep green mountains on the other, seen from the side

scenes.narration: Its capital, Vaduz, has about 5,500 people. A big football stadium can hold ten times that.
scenes.caption: 10X THE TOWN
scenes.picture: A huge packed football stadium glowing under floodlights at night, tens of thousands of cheering fans

scenes.narration: Now rewind to 1699, and meet the Liechtenstein family: rich, powerful, and covered in castles.
scenes.picture: A grand Austrian baroque palace with gardens and fountains in golden afternoon light, noblemen in wigs strolling the path

scenes.narration: But there was a catch. Money alone couldn't buy them a seat in the Imperial Diet's council of princes.
scenes.caption: THE CATCH
scenes.picture: An angry nobleman in a wig and velvet coat standing outside a closed grand wooden door of an imperial hall, arms crossed

scenes.narration: That seat took land answerable directly to the emperor himself.
scenes.caption: THE RULE
scenes.picture: A stern Holy Roman Emperor in ornate robes and crown sits on a throne in a grand hall, nobles bowing before him

scenes.narration: The family already owned huge estates, but the wrong kind, so none of it counted.
scenes.caption: WRONG LAND
scenes.picture: Wide view of vast rolling farmland estates with a manor house and peasants working fields, early 1700s Austria

scenes.narration: So Prince Johann Adam went shopping, hunting for land that fit the rule and whose indebted owners were willing to sell.
scenes.caption: SHOPPING
scenes.picture: A prince in a powdered wig and a clerk in a plain coat review land documents on a wooden desk by candlelight, quill pens and sealed rolls

scenes.narration: In 1699 he found Schellenberg, a mountain lordship so broke its owners were desperate to sell.
scenes.picture: A poor mountain lordship: a crumbling stone manor on a steep hillside with a few sheep, grey clouds, around 1699

scenes.narration: Rocky slopes, thin pastures, a few poor farmers. Not exactly a goldmine.
scenes.caption: POOR LAND
scenes.picture: Close view of a poor Alpine farmer in a rough wool coat leading a thin cow along a stony slope, 1700s

scenes.narration: But it still wasn't enough, so in 1712 he bought a second broke neighbour, the county of Vaduz.
scenes.picture: Aged prince in wig hands a heavy sack of gold coins across a table to a worried count in shabby clothes, 1712

scenes.narration: Two bankrupt scraps of the Alps, bought mainly to qualify for a seat in the Imperial Diet.
scenes.caption: A TICKET
scenes.picture: Two small stone Alpine villages on green hillsides side by side under a bright sky, a river between them, 1700s

scenes.narration: And here's the absurd part: the prince who bought it never set foot in it.
scenes.caption: NEVER VISITED
scenes.picture: A prince in a velvet coat gazes out of a palace window in Vienna at a distant snowy mountain horizon, hands behind his back

scenes.narration: Then in 1719 the emperor merged the two into one principality, and named it after the family.
scenes.picture: Emperor Charles VI in baroque robes signing a decree at an ornate desk, with a wax seal and a quill, courtiers watching

scenes.narration: A country named after a family, bought like a concert ticket. Today it's still the only country named after its ruling family.
scenes.caption: A FAMILY NAME
scenes.picture: Hilltop castle above a small Alpine valley village at sunrise, green meadows and a stone bridge below, 1700s

scenes.narration: The family sent officials to run it, and the first ruling prince actually visited in 1842, over a century later.
scenes.picture: A prince in a top hat and long coat arriving by horse carriage at a small Alpine village, villagers curiously watching, 1842

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, life there was hard, so many villagers packed up and left to find work abroad.
scenes.caption: HARD TIMES
scenes.picture: A poor family with bundles and a handcart walking out of an Alpine village on a dirt road, 1800s, sad faces

scenes.narration: In 1866, during a war between Austria and Prussia, it sent about eighty men to guard its border. According to a popular anecdote, eighty went out and eighty-one came home.
scenes.caption: EIGHTY-ONE
scenes.picture: A cheerful small band of soldiers in 1860s uniforms with one extra smiling man in civilian clothes joining them, returning to a village

scenes.narration: Two years later, in 1868, the little country was so short of cash that it scrapped its army altogether.
scenes.caption: NO ARMY
scenes.picture: A small group of soldiers in 1860s blue uniforms and tall hats laying down their rifles in a stack in a village square

scenes.narration: Then came the First World War, and the empire Liechtenstein leaned on fell apart.
scenes.picture: A grand imperial Austrian building with a flag lowered, crowds of weary people in 1918 coats gathering in the street, grey sky

scenes.narration: The country had used Austria's money, but now that money was melting into worthless paper.
scenes.caption: WORTHLESS
scenes.picture: A man in a 1920s suit holding a huge stack of banknotes in a wheelbarrow, hopeless face, in front of a bakery

scenes.narration: Savings vanished and trade dried up. A tiny, poor country with no army, and nowhere to turn.
scenes.caption: NOWHERE TO TURN
scenes.picture: An empty village market square in 1920s Alps, a lone worried shopkeeper in an apron standing by bare shelves

scenes.narration: So who do you call? The rich, stable neighbour right next door: Switzerland.
scenes.caption: CALL SWITZERLAND
scenes.picture: A Liechtenstein official in a 1920s suit and hat shaking hands with a Swiss official on a stone bridge over the Rhine, mountains behind

scenes.narration: In 1923 they signed a customs treaty with Switzerland, in force from 1924. Goods flowed freely, and the Swiss franc took over as their currency.
scenes.picture: A border post barrier being lifted by a guard in 1920s uniform, a horse cart loaded with goods rolling through, mountains behind

scenes.narration: Overnight, a shaky little country borrowed the credibility of one of the steadiest economies in Europe.
scenes.caption: BORROWED TRUST
scenes.picture: Close view of shiny silver coins and neat stacked banknotes on a wooden counter, a bank clerk's hands in 1920s sleeves

scenes.narration: But steady money alone doesn't make anyone rich. So what did they have to sell?
scenes.caption: WHAT TO SELL?
scenes.picture: A thoughtful government official in a 1920s suit standing at an office window, looking out at a small Alpine town

scenes.narration: Their first answer was rules. In 1926 a law made it cheap and easy to set up a company there.
scenes.caption: 1926 LAW
scenes.picture: Clerks in 1920s suits stamping papers at wooden desks in a bright office, shelves of ledgers behind

scenes.narration: So foreign business owners could park a company, or a family fortune, in a tiny country with light taxes.
scenes.caption: LIGHT TAXES
scenes.picture: A businessman in a suit relaxed at a polished desk, a small model of a bright mountain town beside a stack of gold coins

scenes.narration: Each company paid fees, and historically, those fees helped keep taxes low for everyone else.
scenes.caption: FEES ADD UP
scenes.picture: A stream of golden coins pouring from many small paper envelopes into one big wooden treasure chest in a bright room

scenes.narration: Today the company tax rate is about twelve and a half percent. Germany and Austria charge much more.
scenes.caption: 12.5% TAX
scenes.picture: Two scales side by side, one with a small pile of coins and one with a huge pile, set on a clean desk in a bright office

scenes.narration: Next came banks. The princely family even owns one, LGT, among the biggest family-owned private banks around.
scenes.caption: BANKING
scenes.picture: A modern glass bank building in a small Alpine town, sunlight on its windows, well-dressed people walking in, mountains behind

scenes.narration: Then comes the weird one. One surprising contributor is dental products.
scenes.caption: DENTAL
scenes.picture: Close view of a technician's gloved hands holding a gleaming set of white dentures under a bright lab light

scenes.narration: A company there, Ivoclar, sells crowns and fillings worldwide.
scenes.caption: IVOCLAR
scenes.picture: A dentist and a smiling patient in a bright clinic, a tray of white crowns and tools on a table

scenes.narration: And then there are tools. In 1941 two brothers, Martin and Eugen Hilti, started a small workshop in Schaan.
scenes.caption: HILTI, 1941
scenes.picture: Two young men in work aprons in a small 1940s metal workshop, one at a lathe, the other examining a part, warm lamp light

scenes.narration: Their drills and nail guns now power building sites around the world.
scenes.caption: HILTI TOOLS
scenes.picture: A construction worker in a hard hat drilling into concrete on a skyscraper site, sparks of dust, tall cranes behind

scenes.narration: Here's a number that shows how big it grew: there are roughly as many jobs there as people living there.
scenes.caption: 40,000 JOBS
scenes.picture: A busy morning crowd of office and factory workers walking along a small Alpine town street towards modern buildings

scenes.narration: So every morning, thousands of workers pour in from Switzerland and Austria just to clock in.
scenes.caption: COMMUTERS
scenes.picture: A line of cars and a commuter train crossing a river bridge in the early morning, mountains and mist behind

scenes.narration: Add it up, and GDP per person is more than double America's, though all those commuters inflate that number.
scenes.caption: RICHEST
scenes.picture: A neat, wealthy Alpine town street with expensive cars, flower boxes, and smiling residents on a sunny day

scenes.narration: And stamps! Collectors worldwide love Liechtenstein's tiny, beautiful stamps, and that's yet another small income stream.
scenes.caption: STAMPS
scenes.picture: Close view of a collector's hands with tweezers placing a colorful stamp into a page, magnifying glass nearby

scenes.narration: One more trick helps: with no army, it spends nothing on soldiers, tanks, or planes.
scenes.caption: ZERO ARMY
scenes.picture: A peaceful green valley with grazing cows and a small stone town, a white dove flying across a blue sky

scenes.narration: Switzerland represents it in many places abroad and handles customs, so the big neighbour does the heavy lifting.
scenes.caption: BIG NEIGHBOUR
scenes.picture: A friendly border officer in a uniform waving a car through a mountain road crossing, tall peaks behind

scenes.narration: So the country's rich. But here's the real question: who actually runs this place?
scenes.caption: WHO RULES?
scenes.picture: A hilltop castle above a small town at dusk, a single golden window lit, mountains darkening behind

scenes.narration: Not a figurehead. The ruling family lives in the castle above Vaduz, and the prince's powers are real.
scenes.caption: THE PRINCE
scenes.picture: Vaduz-style hilltop castle with stone walls and a tower above green slopes, golden afternoon light

scenes.narration: He can veto any law that parliament passes. And he can even dismiss the government.
scenes.caption: VETO POWER
scenes.picture: A distinguished prince in a dark suit at a long desk firmly holding up a hand to stop a stack of papers

scenes.narration: In 2003, voters were asked to give him even more, and the prince hinted he'd leave if they said no.
scenes.caption: 2003 VOTE
scenes.picture: Citizens in everyday clothes queuing at a small village polling station with a wooden ballot box, sunny day

scenes.narration: Nearly two thirds voted yes. In an age of republics, a tiny country chose a more powerful prince.
scenes.caption: 64% YES
scenes.picture: Cheerful townspeople clapping in a village square with a castle on the hill behind them, sunny day

scenes.narration: And the family fortune keeps growing, with one of Europe's great private art collections on top.
scenes.caption: ART TREASURES
scenes.picture: A grand palace gallery with old oil paintings in gold frames lining the walls and polished floors, soft light

scenes.narration: Now for the twist. Remember that seat the prince was after? The family did finally get it, in 1723.
scenes.caption: THE TWIST
scenes.picture: An empty grand council hall with rows of carved wooden chairs and one single empty chair in the centre, dusty beams of light

scenes.narration: But in 1806, with Napoleon reshaping Germany, the Empire itself ended, and the seat vanished with it.
scenes.picture: Napoleon in his bicorne hat and grey coat on horseback in front of French soldiers on a hill, battle smoke on the horizon, 1806

scenes.narration: The vote was gone, but the land they'd bought was still there, and it stayed in the family's hands.
scenes.caption: LAND STAYED
scenes.picture: A quiet green Alpine valley with a small village and church spire, golden evening light, 1806

scenes.narration: So Liechtenstein became a sovereign state, almost by accident, and later fully independent.
scenes.caption: BY ACCIDENT
scenes.picture: Villagers in 1800s clothing cheering around a raised flag pole in a mountain village square, bright sky

scenes.narration: A shopping trip for a vote, a Swiss tie, and smart company and trade policy built one of the richest nations on Earth.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: Sweeping view of a prosperous small Alpine country at sunset, castle on the hill, modern town glowing below, snowy peaks beyond

scenes.narration: Not bad for a country that started as a receipt nobody checked.
scenes.caption: A RECEIPT
scenes.picture: Warm sunset light over the Alpine valley, a lone old stone castle on a hill glowing amber above a peaceful town

description:
Why is Liechtenstein, a tiny country in the Alps with about 40,000 people, one of the richest places on Earth? How a prince bought two broke lordships just to win a seat among the emperor's princes, a seat that vanished in 1806, then built wealth from low company taxes, banking, dental products and Hilti tools.

The full story of Liechtenstein, the Swiss customs treaty and franc, and why a prince still holds real power today.

Sources: Historical Lexicon of the Principality of Liechtenstein (historisches-lexikon.li); Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Liechtenstein"; Princely House of Liechtenstein official history; Liechtenstein Institute publications.

short.title: The Prince Who Bought a Country He Never Saw
short.description:
How tiny Liechtenstein went from a bought seat that vanished to one of the richest countries on Earth. A quick story of a prince, a shopping trip and a Swiss deal.
